title: Naskh
def: Abrogation: the replacing of one ruling by a later one, as God wills.
what: The Quran says that whatever verse God abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He brings one better or similar (2:106). Muslims point to clear cases: the prayer direction changed from Jerusalem to Mecca (2:142–150), and the prohibition of wine came in stages (4:43, then 5:90–91).

The term is mainly about rulings of law. Later scholars cut the number of cases drastically: al-Suyuti kept about twenty, and Shah Waliullah five. Some, such as Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, denied abrogation within the Quran altogether.
misread: That Muhammad cancelled the peaceful verses with violent ones, so Islam is violent.
sources: Some early exegetes made sweeping claims that one verse cancelled many. Many scholars rejected this, and the principles the Quran repeats are not treated as cancelled: no compulsion in religion (2:256), kindness and justice to those who have not fought you over your religion (60:8), and the command to deal fairly even with those one dislikes (5:8).

title: Nation of Islam
def: An American movement founded in the 1930s whose beliefs, including that a man was God in person, are not accepted by mainstream Muslims.
what: Wallace D. Fard Muhammad began teaching in Detroit in 1930, and Elijah Muhammad (1897–1975) led the movement from 1934 until his death. Its teachings on race and on Fard’s divinity differ from Islam, which holds that God is one and that Muhammad was the last prophet. Malcolm X left it in 1964, made the pilgrimage, and spoke of seeing Muslims of every colour praying together.
sources: In 1975 Elijah Muhammad’s son, Warith Deen Mohammed, led most followers into mainstream Sunni Islam. Louis Farrakhan revived the Nation in 1978. The Five Percent Nation was founded in Harlem in 1964 by Clarence 13X, who had been a Nation member, and it has its own teachings.

title: No compulsion in religion
def: “There is no compulsion in religion” (2:256): faith cannot be forced.
what: “There is no compulsion in religion; right guidance has become clear from error” (2:256). “If your Lord had willed, all who are on earth would have believed. Would you then compel people to be believers?” (10:99). “Say: the truth is from your Lord; so let whoever wishes believe, and whoever wishes disbelieve” (18:29). Commentators relate 2:256 to Ansari parents who had raised their sons as Jews and wanted to make them Muslims (Abu Dawud).
misread: That the verse was cancelled by the verses on fighting.
sources: A few commentators said 2:256 was abrogated by 9:5 or 9:73, but most hold that it stands, as a general principle that no one may be forced to believe, and as an assertion that faith done under compulsion is without worth. The Prophet’s own constitution at Medina left the Jews their religion (Ibn Ishaq).

title: Noah
def: Noah, the prophet who called his people for 950 years and was saved from the flood in the ark.
what: Chapter 71 is named for him. He called his people night and day (71:5–9), and God told him to build an ark (11:37–38). He stayed among them “a thousand years less fifty” (29:14). When the flood came he saved a pair of every kind (11:40). His son refused to board and drowned (11:42–43). The ark came to rest on al-Judi (11:44).
sources: The Quran presents the flood as a punishment for a people who rejected a prophet, and does not say it covered the whole earth, though many commentators took it so. Noah is among the five greatest messengers, and Muslims give him their salutation of peace (37:79).

title: Nabiyy
def: A prophet: one who receives God’s message word for word, is ordered to convey it, and exemplifies its precepts in his own life; plural anbiyā’.
what: A nabiyy is a person chosen by God to receive a message from Him word for word, with the express order to convey it to people and to show its precepts in his own life. The plural is anbiyā’. The Quran names many of them, from Adam and Noah to Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad (peace be upon them all). The Quran calls Muhammad the seal of the prophets (33:40). Muslims therefore hold that prophethood ended with him, and that every earlier prophet brought the same call to worship God alone. A nabiyy is distinguished in common usage from a rasūl, the bearer of a message to a people, although the two words often overlap.
misread: That “prophet” in English means a foreteller of the future, when the Arabic word is about receiving and delivering revelation.

title: Na'iman
def: “May you be blessed.” It is said to a person who has just bathed, shaved or had a haircut.
what: Naʿīman is a short good wish said to a person who has just finished a bath, a shave or a haircut. It carries the sense of comfort and well-being, and the speaker is wishing that the freshness and ease of the moment be a blessing for the other person. It is a courtesy of everyday life. A Muslim who sees a friend or relative freshly groomed says it as a greeting, and the one addressed answers with a prayer of his own for the speaker. It belongs with the many ordinary expressions by which Muslims turn small occasions into a remembrance of God’s favour.

title: Nasikh, al-
def: The verses of the Quran whose content revokes a ruling or meaning in another verse, which is then called al-mansūkh.
what: Al-Nāsikh is the abrogating verse: a verse of the Quran whose content has removed a ruling given in another verse. The verse that is superseded is called al-mansūkh. The scholars of the Quran treat it as a matter of the order in which God revealed His commands to a growing community. The principle rests on the Quran’s own statement that whatever verse God abrogates or causes to be forgotten, He replaces with one better or like it (2:106; see also 16:101). Scholars have differed on how many verses are affected, and many have narrowed the number a great deal.
misread: That abrogation shows the Quran contradicting itself, when it describes a staged revelation to a community.
sources: Knowing which verse is earlier and which later is a condition for those who derive rulings from the Quran. It depends on the circumstances of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl) and on reports from the Companions of the Prophet.

title: Nasikh al-Hadith wa Mansukhuhu
def: The science that studies hadith whose content revokes the meaning of other hadith, or that were themselves revoked by them.
what: This science examines pairs of hadith in which a later report has cancelled the ruling of an earlier one. The hadith that revokes is the nāsikh and the one revoked is the mansūkh. The aim is to know which of two apparently conflicting reports from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) applies, so that a ruling is not drawn from a report whose ruling was later withdrawn. Scholars establish the order by the words of the Prophet himself, by the statement of a Companion, or by dating the reports through the events they describe. The topic is linked to the study of how the Prophet’s commands changed over the twenty-three years of his mission.
misread: That differing hadith are simply contradictions, when some are earlier rulings that a later one replaced.

title: Nazzala
def: To bring down from heaven to earth, the verb used in the Quran for God’s sending down of revelation.
what: Nazzala is an Arabic verb meaning to bring something down from above, here from heaven to earth. The Quran uses it of God sending down the revelation, as in the verse that speaks of what He has sent down upon His servant (2:23), and of the Book that He sent down to Muhammad (peace be upon him) with the truth (3:3). The verb is a form that carries the sense of repeated or gradual sending down. Muslims cite it for the fact that the Quran came in parts over the years of the Prophet’s mission. The related noun tanzīl names the sending down of revelation.
misread: That revelation is a human composition, when the term describes something sent down from God.
